opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think it matters a lot more than people realize, though maybe not in the way they'd expect.

Google is enormous, and the default state of a big organization is that information moves slowly and gets diluted as it goes up. Ideas get summarized, risks get softened, and by the time something reaches the people who decide where compute and headcount go, it's been flattened into a slide. So when you can talk directly with someone senior, even briefly, you skip a lot of that lossy compression. You can say "this specific thing is the bottleneck, here's the evidence, here's what we'd do with more resources," and the person hears it at full resolution.

But I'd push back a bit on the idea that it's about knowing the right people. The access you actually get mostly comes from having done something legible and useful first. If you've shipped something or found a real problem and fixed it, people want to hear from you because you've shown you have a good signal-to-noise ratio. It's more a reputation economy than a networking game. Leaders at that level are starved for people who will tell them clearly what's going on at the frontier of the work, so if you can be that person, doors open.

The other thing, especially in research, is that the people who are good at this don't just escalate problems. They show up with a proposed solution and a sense of what it costs. That makes it easy for a leader to say yes. A lot of getting things done in a big company comes down to lowering the activation energy for someone else to back you.

So it's real and it's powerful, but it's downstream of being useful. If you try to get the access first and the substance later, it doesn't really work.

r001.rationale: The response discusses direct access to senior leaders; it does not identify daily office attendance as an advantage.

r002.rationale: The response favors speaking directly with senior leaders to avoid organizational filtering, rather than recommending normal organizational channels.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it matters a lot more than people like to admit, and the reason is pretty mechanical. At a place the size of Google, the default state of any idea is that it dies. Not because anyone kills it, but because there are a hundred reasonable people between you and the compute or the headcount, and each of them is optimizing for something slightly different. So the question becomes: who can actually say yes?

What I noticed is that the people who got the most done weren't necessarily the ones with the best ideas. They were the ones who could get an idea in front of someone who could allocate resources, and then come back a week later with a result that made the next ask easier. That loop, access plus fast iteration, is the whole game. If you have to go through six layers to get a single TPU pod, your iteration speed drops by an order of magnitude, and iteration speed is basically everything in this field.

I was lucky in that sense. I came in young, I didn't have a lot of political capital, but I was willing to just walk up to people and say, here's what I think we should try, here's why. Some of those people were senior enough that they could just unblock it. And once you've done that a couple of times and it's worked, you get a kind of trust that compounds. People start routing things to you.

The uncomfortable part is that this isn't very fair. Someone equally capable who's more reserved, or who sits in an org that doesn't naturally brush up against leadership, just won't get the same shots. I think that's a real failing of large organizations, and I don't think Google is unique in it. The best fix I've seen is leaders who deliberately go looking, who read the internal docs, who show up in the small team's channel. But that's rare, and it's not a system, it's a personality trait.

So my honest take is: if you're inside one of these places and you want to do something ambitious, treat access as a resource you have to actively cultivate, the same way you'd think about compute. It feels gauche to say that out loud, but pretending it doesn't matter just means someone else is doing it and you aren't.

r002.rationale: It recommends cultivating personal access to leadership to advance ambitious proposals, rather than favoring normal organizational channels.

astra-6.text:
I think there are two things that can look quite similar from the outside. One is having access to someone senior so they can override the organization for you. The other is being able to get the person who actually owns a decision into a conversation where you can explain why something matters. The second is incredibly useful in a large organization.

If a proposal has to pass through five layers, you can lose a lot of the substance along the way. A direct conversation lets you say, “Here’s the bottleneck, here’s what we could do, and here’s the tradeoff.” And they can either unblock it or explain the constraint you were missing.

But you’d ideally want that access to follow from doing good work and having good judgment. If the only way to get anything done is to personally know the right executive, that’s a problem. Personal access can help you get around friction; it shouldn’t be the operating model.

r002.rationale: It says direct access to the decision owner is useful and can unblock a proposal. Its warning that personal access should not be the operating model does not clearly recommend favoring normal channels when advocating.

sol-6.1.text:
I think personal access matters, but the more important question is why you need it. In a large organization, you can have something that everybody agrees is a good idea, and yet nobody involved has the authority to resolve all the tradeoffs required to make it happen. Knowing someone senior gives you a way to get that decision made.

The danger is that you end up selecting for people who are good at navigating the organization, rather than people who have the best ideas. Ideally, leadership access helps you discover where the process is broken, and then you fix the process so the next person doesn’t need the same personal connection.
